c.tagline: A remote oasis at the edge of Tassili n'Ajjer, home to some of the world's oldest and largest collections of prehistoric rock art

taxi.fareNote: Tassili n'Ajjer excursions require a licensed guide and permit, arranged in advance through a tour agency

emergency.note: Dial 17 for police and 14 for medical/fire emergencies; French is more useful than English with dispatchers

solo.f: escorted tours only; town itself safe

hood_landmark.Djanet Old Town: Djanet's palm-shaded old town and market

avoid.reason: Independent travel outside town is restricted — the desert toward the Libyan and Niger borders is off-limits, and Tassili n'Ajjer excursions require licensed local guides.

hood_desc: The small palm-oasis town center with most hotels, the market, and Tuareg craft shops; the base for organizing any expedition.

Djanet's southern quarter, strung along the RN3 as it climbs out of the oasis towards Tiska airport and the Tadrart. It is quieter and more spread out than the centre, with a couple of the town's best-known hotels built into the rocks above the road; a car or a lift into town is useful.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water; desert supplies can be brackish or untreated.

transit.hours: Daylight hours; desert travel is carefully planned around heat and light
transit.pay: Arranged in advance with a tour agency, typically pre-paid
transit.map: Not applicable; all excursions are guide-led
transit.note: Visiting Tassili n'Ajjer legally requires a registered guide and park permit

airport.name: Djanet Inedbirene Airport
airport.note: ~30 km (40 min) from town. Pre-arranged guide or hotel transfer.
airport.taxiEst: No route fare is published for this airport; the taxi figure is estimated from Algeria's official taxi tariff (40 DZD base plus 50 DZD/km) over 30 km, not from a quoted fare.

tip.s: 10-15% is customary and expected for trekking guides
tip.r: Rounding up or 5-10% is appreciated, not obligatory

food.name: Taguella
food.desc: The Tuareg desert bread: a thick semolina disc buried in hot sand and embers to bake, then broken into pieces and soaked in a spiced meat and vegetable sauce.

places.name: Cafe Touareg
places.note: Known locally for taguella and strong coffee; the easiest place to try it without a desert trip.

places.name: Tadrart and Tassili desert camps
places.area: Dunes south and east of Djanet
places.note: Guides bake taguella in the sand at the evening fire; the way it is meant to be eaten.

places.name: Hotel Tadrart
places.note: Simple hotel dining room and rooftop terrace serving Tuareg staples to trekkers.

food.name: Mechoui
food.desc: Whole lamb or goat rubbed with cumin and salt and roasted slowly over coals or in a sand pit until the meat pulls away from the bone.

places.name: Le Petit Sahara
places.note: Town restaurant singled out in recent guides for its slow-roasted mechoui.

places.name: Tassili Campement
places.note: Camp kitchen roasts whole lamb for groups; arrange in advance with your guide.

places.name: Tadrart desert camps
places.note: Multi-day trek operators cook mechoui on the final night under the dunes.

food.name: Saharan couscous
food.desc: Hand-rolled semolina steamed over a broth of lamb or goat with carrot, turnip, chickpeas and courgette, the standard shared plate at any Djanet table.

places.name: Le Petit Sahara
places.note: Dependable full couscous plates at lunch, often the day's set meal.

places.name: Hotel Tadrart
places.note: Hotel restaurant serving couscous nightly to guests and walk-ins.

places.name: Tassili Campement
places.note: Eco-camp with solar showers and a kitchen doing couscous and stews for trekkers.

food.name: Molokhia and desert stews
food.desc: Goat stewed with ground molokhia leaves into a dark, glossy sauce, eaten with bread or couscous; a Saharan crossover dish found across Djanet.

places.name: Cafe Touareg
places.note: Home-style cooking with whatever stew is on that day; ask what the pot holds.

places.name: Le Petit Sahara
places.note: Rotates goat and lamb stews alongside grills; generous portions for the price.

places.name: Family guesthouses, Adjahil ksar
places.note: Guesthouses in the old ksour cook family stews for guests on request.

food.name: Oasis dates and goat cheese
food.desc: Dates from Djanet's palm groves eaten fresh or dried with dry curd goat cheese and a handful of nuts; the standard offering to any arriving guest.

places.name: Djanet central market
places.note: Stalls sell several date varieties by the kilo along with cheese, nuts and spices.

places.name: El Mihan and Azelouaz palm groves
places.note: Growers in the old ksour gardens sell dates straight from the palms in autumn.

places.name: Hotel Tadrart
places.note: Dates and cheese come with tea on the rooftop terrace at sunset.

food.name: Tuareg tea
food.desc: Green tea boiled with sugar and poured from height into small glasses three times, the rounds said to run bitter, then gentle, then sweet.

places.name: Cafe Touareg
places.note: Everyday tea and coffee stop where the ritual is done over embers. No alcohol is sold anywhere in Djanet.

places.name: Hotel Tadrart
places.note: Rooftop terrace made for sunset mint tea over the oasis.

places.name: Tadrart desert camps
places.note: Guides brew the three rounds on the fire after dinner; the core Tuareg hospitality ritual.

food.name: Eghajira and camel milk
food.desc: Eghajira is a festive Tuareg drink of pounded millet, dates, goat cheese and water; fresh camel or goat milk is the other desert staple.

places.name: Djanet central market
places.note: Milk and the millet, date and cheese ingredients are sold here; ask vendors who makes it.

places.name: Sebiba festival gatherings
places.note: Eghajira is prepared for the spring Sebiba celebrations and other Tuareg feasts.

places.name: Tuareg desert camps
places.note: Camel milk is offered at nomad camps along trekking routes; drink it fresh.

landmarks: Tassili n'Ajjer National Park
A UNESCO plateau of wind-carved sandstone forests sheltering some 15,000 prehistoric rock paintings and engravings, among Earth's greatest open-air art galleries.
Sefar
Deep on the Tassili plateau, this labyrinth of rock cities holds the famed Great God of Sefar and thousands of luminous prehistoric paintings.
Jabbaren
One of the richest rock-art sites in the Sahara, its 'giants' and herding scenes chronicling millennia when the desert was green savanna.
Tegharghart (The Crying Cow)
A tender Neolithic engraving of weeping cattle etched into a boulder near Djanet, mourning, legend says, the Sahara's vanished waters.
Tadrart Rouge
South of Djanet, crimson dunes lap surreal sandstone towers in Algeria's most photogenic desert, glowing impossibly red at sunset.
Tin Merzouga Dune
The queen of the Tadrart, a giant apricot-coloured star dune whose crest rewards climbers with oceanic views over red sands.
Erg Admer
A sea of golden dunes rolling just outside Djanet, the classic spot for camel treks, sandboarding and blazing Saharan sunsets.
Essendilene Canyon
A palm-fringed gorge hiding a permanent guelta pool beneath towering cliffs, the storybook oasis of countless Tuareg legends.
Djanet Oasis and Old Ksour
Three ancient mud-brick villages, including hillside Azellouaz and El Mihan, overlook lush palm gardens threaded by irrigation channels in the oasis heart.
Tikoubaouine
A gathering of natural sandstone arches and mushroom rocks in the Tadrart desert, a favourite camp spot beneath extraordinary starry skies.

train.note: There is no railway in the Algerian Sahara. SNTF's network (https://www.sntf.dz/) is confined to the north of the country, some 2,000 km away. Djanet is reached by air from Algiers, or by a very long desert drive - most visitors come on organised Tassili n'Ajjer trips that include the flight.

bus.note: No scheduled international coaches - the Libyan and Nigerien borders nearby are closed or unsafe. Check your government's travel advisory before planning any overland movement in this region. Occasional coaches run north toward Illizi and Ouargla, taking a day or more; most travel here is by 4x4 with a guide, which is a legal requirement in the national park.

ferry.note: Djanet is an oasis in the Tassili n'Ajjer plateau in the deep Sahara with no navigable water, so there are no ferries.

full.name: Bordj El Haouas
full.blurb: Small Saharan crossroads town north of Djanet surrounded by dramatic sandstone rock formations along the route toward Illizi.

notes.walk: The oasis town itself is small and walkable; Tassili n'Ajjer and the Tadrart require a multi-day guided trek or 4x4 expedition
notes.safety: Requires a licensed guide and permits for Tassili n'Ajjer excursions; check current travel advisories for far southeastern Algeria before visiting. Low crime in town; the main risks are desert travel logistics and remoteness.
notes.net: Limited 3G in town, no coverage in Tassili n'Ajjer. Wifi available in a few hotels but often slow or absent. ~$5-10 for a prepaid tourist SIM (passport required to register). Wifi limited to a handful of hotels. A Mobilis or Djezzy prepaid SIM, registered with your passport.
notes.transit: No formal transit; travel is by licensed 4x4 guide vehicles
notes.transport: Djanet Inedbirene Airport (VVZ), about 30 km from town, with domestic flights from Algiers. No passenger rail service. Very limited long-distance bus service; most visitors fly in. Remote desert roads; independent driving without a guide is not recommended.

laundry.note: A few self-service laveries in Algiers; no published rates
